# A1. CPU matmul ladder generated by the compiler

<p class="page-intro">This case study asks whether the Vortex compiler can take the naive matrix multiplication from v0.1 and, using only its own passes, climb toward the speed of a tuned BLAS library while keeping every bit of the answer the language promises. The method is fixed on this page now; the tables stay empty until the work is measured.</p>

<p class="vx-meta">Status: Not started · Planning size: M to L</p>

## The question

How close can compiler-generated single-precision matrix multiplication come
to Apple's Accelerate library on the same machine, with the same shapes and
the same number of threads, when every step is produced by a Vortex pass from
the unchanged source of
[stage 10](../../compiler/guide/stage-10-matrix-multiplication.md)?

Each step is a **rung**: the previous rung plus one transformation. The whole
sequence, from the naive triple loop to the fastest version, is the
**ladder**. A rung is **strict** when it obeys Vortex's default
floating-point rule, which forbids any transformation that changes a result
the specification fixes
([types and values, 4.4](../../specification/types-and-values.md#44-floating-point-values)).

When the work is done, this section will hold one sentence of this form, with
every blank filled from the tables below:

> On ___, for a ___ × ___ × ___ multiplication, the compiler's fastest strict
> rung runs at ___ GFLOP/s (95% confidence interval ___ to ___), which is ___%
> of Accelerate on the same number of cores and ___% of the measured strict
> peak, with output bitwise identical to the naive loop.

## Why employers care

Teams that build compilers for CPUs and kernels for accelerators look for two
skills together: knowing how a compiler transforms loops, and proving a
speedup with measurements and a model of the machine. CPU compiler
performance work means reading generated machine code for missed
optimizations, then improving loop transformations and vectorization. Kernel
work means placing a result against a roofline or a similar model and
explaining the gap that remains.

Public write-ups of fast matrix multiplication usually show the second skill
without the first. Boehm's CPU worklog, for example, rewrites a C++ kernel by
hand at each step, compiles it with `-ffast-math`, and compares the result
with Intel's MKL called through NumPy.[^boehm] That is a good tutorial and a
different piece of work. In this study the source never changes: the compiler
produces every rung, each rung comes with a test showing its transformation
was legal, and the answer stays exact. It shows both skills in one place,
which a hand-written ladder cannot.

## What to build

The ladder follows the well-trodden path from naive loops to a BLAS-style
kernel. Goto and van de Geijn's layered design keeps a packed block of one
input in the L2 cache, streams packed panels of the other through the L1
cache, and holds a small block of the output in registers.[^goto] BLIS
reorganizes the same idea as loops around one small **micro-kernel**, the
only part written for a particular processor.[^blis] The rungs below reach
that design one transformation at a time.

Chapter ids refer to the [optimization book](../../optimize/index.md).

| Rung | Transformation | Keeps the bits? | Taught in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | None: the v0.1 triple loop, with its bounds and overflow checks | Baseline | [Stage 10](../../compiler/guide/stage-10-matrix-multiplication.md) |
| 1 | Scalar cleanup: constant folding, dead-code removal, redundant address arithmetic removed, checks deleted only where a range proof exists | Yes | O5 to O8 |
| 2 | Loop interchange from i-j-k to i-k-j, so the inner loop walks `B` and `C` along rows | Yes | [P7](../../optimize/p7-loop-transformations.md) |
| 3 | Vectorization along `j` with NEON | Yes, if no multiply-add is fused | P10 |
| 4 | Cache tiling, with tile sizes derived from the machine's cache sizes | Yes, if `C` is accumulated in place and the `k` tiles run in order | P8 |
| 5 | Packing blocks of `A` and panels of `B` into contiguous buffers | Yes: packing only copies | P12 |
| 6 | Register-blocked micro-kernel: unroll-and-jam, accumulators held in registers | Yes, if the accumulators start from the loaded `C` tile | P12 |
| 7 | Fused multiply-add | No: allowed only when the program opts in | P11 |
| 8 | Multithreading over blocks of `i` or `j` | Yes, as long as `k` is never split across threads | P13 |
| 9 | Block sizes chosen by a model or by search | Yes, if the search space holds only bit-preserving variants | P15 and [A9](cost-model-autotuner.md) |
| Stretch | SME outer-product instructions, on chips that have them | Depends on the mode used | The [back-end book](../../backend/index.md); Remke and Breuer show SME matrix kernels[^hellosme] |

The "Keeps the bits?" column follows from one observation. For each element
`C[i][j]`, the naive loop adds the products in increasing `k`, one at a time,
into a running value. A transformation keeps the bits exactly when it keeps
that order for every element. Interchange, vectorizing across `j`, tiling
with in-place accumulation, packing, and splitting `i` or `j` across threads
all change the order *between* elements, never *within* one. A fused
multiply-add rounds once where the separate operations round twice, and
splitting `k` across threads regroups the sum, so both can change the last
bits of a result.

Around the rungs, the work includes:

- a way to choose the pass list for each rung, so that every rung is the same
  source compiled with a different set of passes;
- a remark from each pass that says what it did, or why it declined, as the
  [philosophy](../../philosophy.md#6-explain-performance-decisions) asks;
- for each pass, a legality test that shows the transformation in the IR, and
  a negative test with a loop nest the pass must refuse, for example one
  whose dependences forbid interchange;
- a baseline program in C++ that calls Accelerate's `cblas_sgemm`,[^accelerate]
  held to one thread with `BLASSetThreading`, which the vecLib header
  `thread_api.h` in the macOS SDK declares for macOS 15 and later (checked in
  the SDK on 2026-09-23);
- ceiling microbenchmarks for peak arithmetic with separate multiplies and
  adds, peak arithmetic with fused multiply-adds, and memory bandwidth, built
  as [P1](../../optimize/p1-measure-first.md) and P3 describe.

This study leaves out:

- hand-written kernels in C or assembly for any rung (the baseline and the
  microbenchmarks are separate programs, not rungs);
- fast-math modes of any kind;
- GPU code, which is [A8](gpu-matmul-ladder.md) and chapter
  [G10](../../gpu/g10-matmul-ladder.md);
- a general cost model, which is [A9](cost-model-autotuner.md). Rung 9 may
  use a plain grid search.

The capstone chapter, [P16](../../optimize/p16-capstone.md), walks the same
ladder as a set of exercises; this page is where the results of doing them
are reported.

## Method

Every timing follows [How Vortex performance is measured](../measuring.md),
and every correctness check follows [How Vortex is tested](../testing.md).
This section says what is specific to the ladder.

### What is compared with what

- **Each rung with rung 0.** Same source, same compiler commit; only the
  enabled passes differ. The comparison covers the output bits and the time.
- **Each rung with Accelerate.** `cblas_sgemm` runs on the same shapes, the
  same single-precision data and the same number of threads: one thread for
  every rung except 8, and all performance cores for rung 8. BLAS computes
  `C = α·A·B + β·C`;[^boehm] the baseline sets α and β so that it does
  exactly the work the Vortex program does.
- **Each rung with the machine's ceilings.** The **roofline model** bounds a
  kernel's speed by the smaller of two limits: the processor's peak
  arithmetic rate, and the memory bandwidth multiplied by the kernel's
  **operational intensity**, the number of floating-point operations it
  performs per byte it moves to and from memory.[^roofline] Every rung
  becomes a point on that chart, and a rung that helps moves its point up.

Two arithmetic ceilings matter here, not one. Vortex's default rule forbids
fusing a multiply and an add, so the honest ceiling for every strict rung is
the peak rate of separate multiplies and adds. The fused ceiling applies only
to rung 7. Measuring both shows the price of strictness on this machine.
Hoefler and Belli ask for this kind of upper bound next to any measured
result, so that a reader can judge how far from the limit it is.[^hb]

An M × N × K multiplication performs $2MNK$ floating-point operations: each of
the $MN$ outputs takes $K$ multiplications and $K$ additions. The rate is

$$
\text{GFLOP/s} = \frac{2MNK}{t \times 10^{9}}
$$

where $t$ is the median time of one multiplication, in seconds.

### The correctness gate

No rung is timed until it passes the gate. The gate runs the rung and rung 0
on the same inputs and compares the output matrices. For every rung marked
"Yes" in the table above, the comparison is bitwise. For rung 7 it uses a
tolerance chosen before the run, by the reasoning in
[stage 10](../../compiler/guide/stage-10-matrix-multiplication.md#comparing-with-a-known-answer).
The inputs include stage 10's small whole numbers and also values drawn from
a fixed seed whose sums round, because only inexact inputs reveal a reordered
sum.

### Machines

Every number comes from the owner's Apple M4 Pro. Cache sizes and core counts
are queried from the machine with `sysctl`, not copied from a specification
sheet, and recorded in the setup table. Apple documents that a task's
quality-of-service class influences which kind of core runs it,[^apple-tuning]
so the benchmark sets its class explicitly and records it. A second machine
is welcome; it gets its own setup and results tables.

### What counts as success

1. Every rung is produced by the compiler from the unchanged stage 10 source.
   No rung is hand-written.
2. Every rung passes the correctness gate on every shape, and every rung
   marked "Yes" is bitwise identical to rung 0.
3. Every number is measured under the protocol, with its confidence interval
   and its raw data in the repository.
4. The gap between the fastest strict rung and Accelerate, and between that
   rung and the strict ceiling, is measured and explained with counters, IR
   or assembly.
5. A numeric target is written below before the first measurement, and the
   result is reported whether or not it meets the target.

Target, written before the first run: ___

### Ceilings

| Ceiling | How it is measured | Threads | Value | Unit | Raw data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strict arithmetic peak | Independent multiplies and adds, no fusing | 1 |  | GFLOP/s |  |
| Strict arithmetic peak | Independent multiplies and adds, no fusing | All performance cores |  | GFLOP/s |  |
| Fused multiply-add peak | Independent fused multiply-adds | 1 |  | GFLOP/s |  |
| Fused multiply-add peak | Independent fused multiply-adds | All performance cores |  | GFLOP/s |  |
| Memory bandwidth | Streaming triad over arrays larger than the last cache | 1 |  | GB/s |  |
| Memory bandwidth | Streaming triad over arrays larger than the last cache | All performance cores |  | GB/s |  |
| Ridge point | Strict peak divided by bandwidth | 1 |  | FLOP/byte |  |
| Ridge point | Strict peak divided by bandwidth | All performance cores |  | FLOP/byte |  |

The **ridge point** is the operational intensity at which a kernel stops
being limited by memory and starts being limited by arithmetic.[^roofline]

### Shapes

| Shape | M | N | K | Why it is included |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small |  |  |  | All three matrices fit in the L1 data cache. |
| Medium |  |  |  | They fit in L2 but not in L1. |
| Large |  |  |  | They are larger than the last cache. |
| Rectangular |  |  |  | M, N and K all differ. |
| Ragged |  |  |  | No dimension is a multiple of the micro-kernel size, so edge code runs. |

Pass named in the remark
: The pass that produced the rung, as the compiler's own remark names it.

Bits vs rung 0
: "Identical" when every output element matches rung 0 bit for bit;
  otherwise the largest difference found, in units in the last place.

Median time
: The median, over all timed runs, of one full multiplication in
  milliseconds, including any packing and thread start-up that happen inside
  the call.

95% CI
: A 95% confidence interval for the median, computed as the
  [measuring page](../measuring.md) describes.

GFLOP/s
: $2MNK$ divided by the median time, in units of $10^9$ operations per
  second.

% of strict peak
: GFLOP/s divided by the strict arithmetic peak for the same number of
  threads.

% of Accelerate
: GFLOP/s divided by Accelerate's GFLOP/s on the same shape and thread count.

Commit
: The Vortex commit that produced the row.

## What did not work

Empty until work begins. This section will record transformations that were

## Threats to validity

**Measurement bias.** Changing something as unrelated as the size of the
environment variables can move a program's run time enough to reverse a
conclusion, as Mytkowicz and colleagues showed.[^mytk]
[A2](benchmark-harness.md) exists to control this, and the ladder uses its
harness.

**Unequal baselines.** Accelerate may use hardware the Vortex rungs do not.
Boehm attributes Accelerate's lead on an M1 Pro to Apple's matrix
instructions.[^boehm] The results must say whether each side used the matrix
unit. Accelerate is compared as it ships, not with a version handicapped to
match the rungs.

**A reference built with contraction.** If a reference result comes from C++
built with clang, clang fuses multiply-adds within an expression by
default.[^clang-um] A bitwise comparison against that reference compares
against the wrong answer. Every C++ reference is built with contraction off,
and the setup table records the flag.

**Flattering shapes.** Sizes that are multiples of every tile never run edge
code. The ragged shape exists to catch that.

**What the timer includes.** Packing, allocation and thread start-up are part
of the cost. They stay inside the timed region, because Accelerate's time
includes whatever it does internally.

**Checks removed without proof.** Rung 1 may delete a bounds or overflow
check only when it has proved the check can never fail. A rung that is fast
because it dropped a check it could not prove safe is a bug, not a result.
The negative tests include loops where the checks must stay.

**Aliasing assumptions.** Vectorizing at rung 3 relies on the output not
overlapping the inputs, which the
[aliasing rule](../../specification/references.md#98-aliasing) gives for a
mutable reference. The rule leaves some cases to future specification work,
so the pass may rely only on what the rule already guarantees.

**Core placement and heat.** The operating system decides where threads run,
and long runs heat the chip. The setup table records the quality-of-service
class, the power source and the thermal state, and the harness reports when
the spread between runs grows.

**A static split on mixed cores.** Rung 8 divides work between threads. Apple
warns that with a static division, threads on different kinds of core finish
at different times, and recommends distributing work dynamically.[^apple-tuning]
A static split measured on performance cores only must say so.

## Reproduce

Empty until the first measured run. This section will give one command that,
from a clean checkout, builds the compiler, runs the correctness gate, runs
every rung and the baseline under the harness, writes the raw data into the
repository, and regenerates the tables on this page.
